Title: Decentralised Multi-UAV Cooperative Searching Multi-Target in Cluttered and GPS-Denied Environments
Authors: Zhu X., Vanegas F., Gonzalez L.F.
Venue: IEEE Aerospace Conf. (AERO), Big Sky, Montana, Mar 2022, pp. 1-10
Problem Addressed: Multiple UAVs must cooperatively explore, detect and localize several targets in a cluttered, GPS-denied environment (e.g. indoor, urban canyon, cave) with obstacles, under sensing and environment uncertainty.
Method Used: Decentralised Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) framework for multi-agent planning, extended from the authors' earlier single-target POMDP work, paired with online POMDP solvers for sequential decision-making under uncertainty; each UAV shares only limited processed observations and positions with teammates.
UAV/Swarm Type: Multi-rotor UAV team (homogeneous quadrotors), decentralised swarm, simulated team size scaled in experiments
Sensor Type: Onboard range/obstacle sensors and a simulated target-detection sensor model (vision-like) feeding occupancy/belief grids; sensing implemented in ROS/Gazebo
Perception Uncertainty Type: Sensing and environment uncertainty modelled as POMDP observation noise; partial observability of target existence/location and of obstacles in a cluttered map
False Positive Handling: Not explicitly separated from false negatives   uncertainty handled jointly via the POMDP belief update (probabilistic occupancy/target-existence belief rather than binary FP/FN classification)
False Negative Handling: Same as above   false negatives correspond to low-belief/undetected cells in the POMDP belief state, refined as the UAV continues exploring
Confidence Handling: Confidence expressed implicitly as the POMDP belief distribution over target presence per cell/region, updated via Bayesian-style belief propagation as observations accrue
Fusion Method: Decentralised belief sharing: each UAV broadcasts only compressed/processed local observations and pose, which are merged into each agent's own belief representation (not a single centralized map)
Simulation Environment: Robotic Operating System (ROS) + Gazebo simulator; indoor-like cluttered scenarios with obstacles and an a priori known/partially known map
Swarm-Level Metric: Time-cost to find all targets, proportion of search area surveyed, and mission success rate, evaluated as a function of swarm size
Main Result: Multi-UAV decentralised search consistently reduced search time, increased surveyed-area proportion, and improved search-and-rescue success rates as the number of UAVs increased, while avoiding collisions in cluttered, GPS-denied settings.
Limitation: Full text is paywalled (IEEE Xplore); evaluation is simulation-only (ROS/Gazebo), GPS-denied but largely static/known-map indoor scenarios; scalability to large, dynamic, outdoor swarms and to noisy real sensor hardware is not demonstrated.
Relevance to Our Research: Directly relevant as a decentralised cooperative-search baseline under uncertainty (Dec-POMDP belief fusion) for comparison against vision-based detection/fusion methods in the review; illustrates an alternative, non-vision uncertainty-handling paradigm.

Title: Drone swarm strategy for the detection and tracking of occluded targets in complex environments
Authors: Amala Arokia Nathan R.J., Kurmi I., Bimber O.
Venue: Communications Engineering (Nature Portfolio), Vol. 2, Art. 55, Aug 2023
Problem Addressed: Detecting and tracking targets that are heavily occluded by forest vegetation, where conventional single-drone/blind sampling cannot recover sufficient visibility quickly enough for time-critical search-and-rescue.
Method Used: Adaptive real-time Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) that drives drone swarm sampling positions to maximise an anomaly-based visibility objective using Synthetic Aperture (SA)/Airborne Optical Sectioning (AOS) sensing; integrates sequential and parallel multi-drone samples and converts to a default linear scanning pattern when no target is found.
UAV/Swarm Type: Homogeneous rotary-wing drone swarm, simulated swarm sizes of 3, 5 and 10 drones, altitude-staggered for collision avoidance
Sensor Type: Simulated multispectral (RGB + far-infrared/thermal) downward-looking cameras on each drone
Perception Uncertainty Type: Occlusion-induced visibility uncertainty (randomness of vegetation occlusion) and target-motion uncertainty; not sensor-noise/pose-error per se (pose error treated separately as a spatial-sampling-loss term)
False Positive Handling: Implicit: objective function compares contour size of anomaly blob against a fixed visibility threshold (T); samples that do not increase the objective are excluded, limiting spurious detections
False Negative Handling: Implicit: if objective stays below threshold T the swarm reverts to a default scanning pattern, increasing further sampling/integration to recover the target signal rather than declaring failure
Confidence Handling: No explicit confidence/probability score in this paper (later improved in the 2025 follow-up); detection effectively binary against threshold T on the visibility/objective function
Fusion Method: Image-level (pixel) fusion: per-drone images masked by a Reed Xiaoli anomaly detector, then registered to a common reference pose and summed only if the addition increases the visibility objective (conditional integration), with parallel (same-instant) and sequential (cross-time) samples combined
Simulation Environment: WebGL-based procedural forest simulation (ProcTree) with sparse/medium/dense densities (300/400/500 trees/ha), 512x512 px simulated aerial RGB+thermal images, no real-world flight test
Swarm-Level Metric: Maximum Target Visibility (MTV, %) and time-to-converge (s); swarm-size and forest-density sweeps
Main Result: PSO-driven adaptive swarm sampling reached 72% maximum target visibility in 14 s for a 10-drone swarm versus only 51% after 75 s (sequential blind sampling) and 19% after 3 s (parallel blind sampling); larger swarms (n=10 vs 5 vs 3) and sparser forests increased visibility; moving targets were tracked with ~0.59 m position error.
Limitation: Purely simulation-based (no real-world flight validation in this paper); single-target only; confidence/false-positive handling is rudimentary (fixed threshold, no probabilistic confidence metric); assumes centralized image registration and integration.
Relevance to Our Research: Core baseline for swarm-level synthetic-aperture sensing and PSO-based adaptive sampling under occlusion uncertainty; directly comparable to radar/camera fusion approaches and a foundation for the improved confidence-aware 2025 follow-up paper by the same group.

Title: An autonomous drone swarm for detecting and tracking anomalies among dense vegetation
Authors: Amala Arokia Nathan R.J., Strand S., Mehrwald D., Shutin D., Bimber O.
Venue: Communications Engineering (Nature Portfolio), Vol. 4, Art. 205, Nov 2025
Problem Addressed: Field-deployable, fully autonomous drone-swarm detection and tracking of unknown/unclassified anomalous targets (vehicles, lying/standing/walking persons) under heavy forest occlusion, while also coping with real sensor noise (GPS/IMU/compass drift) absent in pure simulation.
Method Used: Centralised adapted Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) using Synthetic Aperture (SA)/Airborne Optical Sectioning (AOS) imaging; introduces a relevance-and-confidence objective function (cluster anomaly-value integral plus ratio-based confidence between the top two candidate clusters) and folds unknown sensor parameters (heading drift, focal-plane orientation) directly into the image-integration process instead of optimising them.
UAV/Swarm Type: 6x DJI Mavic 3T (RGB+thermal) plus 1x DJI Matrice 30T deployment drone; centralised swarm architecture; real field hardware (not simulation)
Sensor Type: Onboard RGB and thermal (FLIR) cameras with RTK GPS for positioning; custom DJI SDK v5.3 application for telemetry/video streaming (~70-120 Mbit/s) to a centralised Windows server
Perception Uncertainty Type: Sensor-pose uncertainty (compass/heading drift of a few degrees, GPS/IMU/pressure-sensor imprecision) compounded with occlusion-induced visibility uncertainty; treated as an (N+3)-dimensional unknown parameter space
False Positive Handling: False positives handled via the new relative confidence metric (target's cluster must be at least twice   threshold T=2   as anomalous as the second-most-anomalous cluster) rather than an absolute, hand-tuned size threshold used in the 2023 legacy method
False Negative Handling: False negatives mainly from temporary target invisibility under locally dense vegetation; quantified directly in the recall metric (false negatives = un-detected target instances) and mitigated by continued PSO-driven re-exploration
Confidence Handling: Explicit confidence metric c = ratio of relevance (anomaly-value integral over cluster area) between the most- and second-most-anomalous clusters, replacing the 2023 paper's contour-size-only metric; confidence threshold T=2 used to decide detection
Fusion Method: Sensor-noise-aware multi-image integration: instead of solving for the true heading/focal-plane parameters, the system integrates many (N+3) n transformed copies of each anomaly mask across a small heading/orientation range, so the correct registration emerges as the location of maximal integrated visibility (avoiding a combinatorially expensive optimisation)
Simulation Environment: Real-world field experiments (not simulation) in sparse/dense forest near Linz, Austria, across 3 experiments: moving vehicle in sparse forest; stationary lying/standing persons in dense forest; two persons walking in dense forest, under low-light/near-dawn conditions
Swarm-Level Metric: Detection precision and recall, average position-estimation error (m), and the new confidence score c, reported per experiment and compared against the 2023 legacy confidence metric
Main Result: Achieved average positional accuracy of 0.39 m with average precision 93.2% and recall 95.9% across experiments; e.g. Experiment I: 93.87% precision / 100% recall / 0.26 m error; Experiment III (moving persons in dense forest): 92.3% precision / 92.3% recall / 0.53 m error; new method outperformed the 2023 legacy confidence metric by ~2-3 percentage points in precision and succeeded in detecting targets the legacy method missed entirely.
Limitation: Only 6 drones used in field tests (smaller than ideal for sensing aperture); detects/tracks only one most-abnormal target at a time (no multi-target capability yet); centralised architecture requires high-bandwidth (70-120 Mbit/s) video/telemetry links, limiting scalability without major network upgrades (5G/6G).
Relevance to Our Research: Highly relevant   state-of-the-art exemplar of explicit confidence-based false positive/negative handling and sensor-noise-aware fusion in a real-world (not just simulated) drone swarm; directly informs how to design confidence metrics and noise-robust fusion for the literature review's target methodology.

Title: Belief States for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
Venue: Department of Computing, Imperial College London (arXiv preprint, Apr 2025)
Problem Addressed: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in partially observable environments, where agents must estimate hidden system state from local histories without centralised data sharing during execution (or even training).
Method Used: Two-stage "Belief-I2Q" framework: (1) self-supervised pre-training of a per-agent Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) that infers a probabilistic belief state (mean + variance) over the true system state from each agent's local observation/action history; (2) the learned belief states are fed into a state-based Q-learning algorithm (an extension of the I2Q decentralised Q-learning method) to train decentralised policies with fully decentralised training and execution (DTDE).
UAV/Swarm Type: Generic multi-agent system (grid-world agents in the experiments)   domain-agnostic framework explicitly motivated by applications including drone management and object search
Sensor Type: Abstracted as agent "observations" in grid-world environments (local visibility radius, asymmetric information) rather than physical camera/radar sensors
Perception Uncertainty Type: Partial observability / information asymmetry between agents, and epistemic uncertainty over the unobserved system state, explicitly quantified as a learned probabilistic distribution (mean and variance) via the CVAE decoder rather than treated as simple sensor noise
False Positive Handling: Not a detection-style false-positive/negative framing   instead, the model encodes uncertainty as variance in the predicted belief distribution; overconfident beliefs are discouraged via the KL-divergence term in the CVAE's variational loss
False Negative Handling: Same mechanism as false positives: residual high variance in the belief distribution signals the unobserved state has not yet been adequately inferred from the agent's history, prompting continued reliance on local Q-learning exploration rather than premature commitment
Confidence Handling: Explicit probabilistic confidence: belief state output as a Gaussian distribution (mean state estimate + log-variance), trained via the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)/CVAE objective, allowing the downstream RL policy to factor in uncertainty rather than treating the belief as a point estimate
Fusion Method: Decentralised, per-agent fusion: each agent's own recurrent history encoder + CVAE produces its private belief state from its own local observation/action history; no central fusion of multiple agents' raw observations (fully DTDE, contrasted with CTDE methods that fuse all agents' data centrally)
Simulation Environment: Custom suite of four grid-world environments (Oracle, Gathering, Escape Room, and the Honeycomb leader-follower paradigm), implemented in PyTorch, evaluated over 3 random seeds
Swarm-Level Metric: Episodic return (reward per episode, smoothed) and convergence speed, compared against recurrent I2Q and recurrent hysteretic independent Q-learning baselines
Main Result: Belief-I2Q outperformed both recurrent baselines in final policy performance on 3 of 4 environments (Oracle, Gathering, Escape Room) and converged faster in Oracle and Escape Room; it underperformed in the Honeycomb environment because the belief model (trained on random rollouts) could not infer the information-asymmetric leader-follower signal needed there.
Limitation: Evaluated only in abstract grid-world domains, not on physical robot/UAV swarms or with real sensor data; requires an initial labelled (fully-observed-state) dataset for pre-training the belief model, which may be costly or unrealistic to obtain in real deployments; fails when state inference requires modelling other agents' policies (information-asymmetry case).
Relevance to Our Research: Highly relevant as a generalisable, decentralised confidence/uncertainty-quantification mechanism (learned belief states with explicit variance) for partially-observable multi-agent perception fusion, applicable in principle to UAV swarm detection-and-tracking tasks as an alternative to hand-crafted confidence metrics.

Title: The influence of limited visual sensing on the Reynolds flocking algorithm
Authors: Enrica Soria, Fabrizio Schiano , Dario Floreano
Venue: 2019 Third IEEE International Conference on Robotic Computing (IRC), Naples, Italy, pp. 138-145
Problem Addressed: Quantifying how a reduction in field of view (FOV) and the orientation of onboard visual sensors degrade the performance of vision-based Reynolds flocking in multi-drone swarms, since most prior flocking work assumes omnidirectional/idealised sensing.
Method Used: we apply a Monte-Carlo method that repeatedly selects random samples of the initial conditions for the flock, i.e. initial positions and velocities of the agents. A batch of 100 simulations is run, and  the final score is the average over the batch.
UAV/Swarm Type: Homogeneous multi-drone swarm (simulation), Reynolds-rule-based decentralised flocking
False Positive Handling: Not explicitly framed as false-positive detections; instead the degradation is measured through reduced order/safety/connectivity, i.e. missed or asymmetric neighbour perception due to narrow FOV is the analogue of "false negatives" on undetected neighbours
False Negative Handling: Quantified indirectly via the "connectivity" and "union" metrics, which capture when an agent loses track of (fails to perceive) flockmates due to limited FOV/orientation, analogous to false-negative neighbour loss
Confidence Handling: No explicit probabilistic confidence score is used; the four custom metrics (order, safety, union, connectivity) act as deterministic, simulation-derived proxies for flocking reliability under different sensing limitations
Fusion Method: Decentralised local rule-based fusion typical of Reynolds flocking   each agent fuses only the relative positions/velocities of neighbours visible within its own limited FOV cone to compute separation/alignment/cohesion velocity commands; no central map or belief fusion
Simulation Environment: MATLAB R2017b software have been used for the simulation, moreover in their simulations, the dynamics of the agents is reproduced in discrete time according to a double integrator mode.
Swarm-Level Metric: Four different swarm metric have been used order, safety, connectivity and union.
Main Result: A decline in the performance of the flock is proportional to a diminution of the width angle ? i.e a reduction in view of the UAV results in decrease of the information they can capture as determined by the union matrix and connectivity metric which also evaluates the gain. However if we look at their order metric then there is a reasonable increase in performance, and this fact is independent of the choice of gain. The results about the safety metric are highly dependent on the Reynolds gains.Moreover, it can be noticed that this metric takes values in a very limited range.
Limitation: The main limitation is only that this hypothesis and experiments  have been done on in a Software i.e in an ideal scenario other different cases  such as noise , environmental factors, interferences have been ignored.Moreover the limited range of the visual sensors and so on.
Relevance to Our Research: This paper provides a fundamental theoretical framework for understanding the minimum hardware constraints (such as camera FOV placement and angles) required to sustain a disorganized swarm. Nonetheless this could also prove beneficial for small camera where our FOV is limited

Title: Vision-Based Neighbor Selection Method for Occlusion-Resilient Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle Swarm Coordination in Three-Dimensional Environments
Venue: Information, Computing and Intelligent Systems, No. 6, pp. 100-117 (Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute)
Problem Addressed: GNSS- and communication-free UAV swarm coordination in 3D environments where visual occlusions between drones (one drone blocking another's line of sight) disrupt decentralised, vision-based flocking, especially in dense formations.
Method Used: Neighbouring Strategies such as Topographic and Delaunay algorithms.
UAV/Swarm Type: Homogeneous quadrotor UAV swarm, simulated swarm sizes of 10-150 agents (point-mass) and up to 70 agents (Gazebo/PX4 quadrotor dynamics)
Perception Uncertainty Type: Occlusion-induced perceptual uncertainty: neighbours fully or partially blocked from an agent's viewpoint by other agents (not environmental clutter), worsening with swarm density
False Positive Handling: Not framed as classification false positives; instead, oversaturation of falsely 'visible' or noisy neighbour counts in dense swarms is mitigated by restricting/selecting which neighbours are used (metric/topological/Delaunay selection) to reduce occlusion-induced noise
False Negative Handling: Quantified via the alignment and union metrics: occluded/undetected neighbours reduce alignment (failure to synchronise velocity) and can reduce union/cohesion (fragmentation into disconnected sub-swarms)   these serve as the paper's proxies for missed (false-negative-like) neighbour information
Confidence Handling: No explicit probabilistic confidence score; reliability is assessed purely through the three deterministic performance metrics (minimum nearest-neighbour distance, alignment, union) averaged over repeated simulation runs (10 runs/configuration, last 25% of steps for steady state)
Fusion Method: Decentralised local fusion: each agent computes an Artificial Potential Field velocity command (social + migration components) using only the relative positions/velocities of its selected (non-occluded, distance/topology/Delaunay-filtered) neighbours   no central map; performance also benchmarked against an idealised "communication-enabled" (all-to-all) condition
Simulation Environment: Two Simulation Environments have been used. The first is the point mass environment implemented in pure Python, where agents are modeled as material points governed by simplified kinematics. Alternatively, the second environment, powered by Gazebo (Gazebo Classic), offers a physics- based simulation. Considering three-dimensional maneuverability, target applications mentioned in Section 1, and market availability, a quadrotor was selected as the drone type for our research.
Swarm-Level Metric: Three swarms metrics have been used Alignment , Minimum Nearest Neighbor Distance and Union
Main Result:
Different results have been determined by the projects.
First is the failure where if the vision of the UAV is affected then there is a severe decline in performance in swarms exceeding 70 agents, causing directional alignment to drop below 0.9 and inter-agent distances to narrow below 0.5 meters, severely risking collisions.
To address this issue the research paper applied different neighbouring regions algorithms from which Topographic strategy effectively maintains high velocity alignment  but is optimal primarily for smaller swarms of up to 50 agents. However Delaunay Strategy provides the best results ensuring perfect alignment and is scalable as well.
Limitation: If we discuss the limitations then this whole situation is again simulated in a software where we are ignoring the environmental and physical conditions as well. Moreover most of the simulations performed are in ideal scenario lacking real world implications.
Relevance to Our Research: The research paper can be utilized for expanding our research in the area of swarm formation and improving it in communication-jammed, or GNSS-denied environments. Moreover it also shows that different issues related to swarm formation can be resolved by using different topological or Delaunay algorithms.
